4.a: (1) Article 29 — protects the right of minorities to conserve their distinct language, script or culture, (2) Article 30 — protects their right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, (3) The tension — the party's demand for one law for all and its opposition to separate personal laws put it in direct conflict with the constitutional guarantee of minority cultural autonomy, (4) The debate — supporters presented uniformity as national integration while opponents read the same stance as majoritarianism. A student who cites only the general equality article misses the specific minority-rights provisions and cannot explain the structural tension with the Constitution's framework.

(1) The 1967 consensus — the Syndicate consulted the Prime Minister and the factions agreed on Dr Zakir Husain, showing the informal negotiation machinery still worked, (2) The 1969 rupture — after the electoral setback the Prime Minister pushed bank nationalisation and the abolition of privy purses against the bosses' wishes, and when the Syndicate nominated its loyalist for President she backed the rival candidate as an independent, asking legislators to vote conscience, (3) The outcome — her candidate won, shifting faction management from accommodation inside party forums to open electoral combat, (4) The structural meaning — the organisational wing lost its veto over a parliamentary leader who commanded a popular mandate, collapsing the Congress system's management mechanism. Treating 1969 as a mere personality clash misses that structural rupture.

6.a: (1) Customary law — no law on Karbi custom or customary justice applies unless the assembly resolves so by a two-thirds majority, (2) Land and resources — transfer stays locally regulated, non-locals need council consent, and mineral and forest royalties are shared with the council, (3) Representation — most seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes, with the Governor holding special responsibility for tribal-area law and order after consulting the ministers, (4) Cultural autonomy — the state decides the medium of instruction up to university level and funds institutions for Karbi language and culture. A poor answer copies the Nagaland article verbatim without adapting land-transfer restrictions, royalty sharing or reserved seats.

3.a: (1) The pattern — Rohan is talkative and outgoing with friends but reserved at a formal school assembly, (2) The situational reading — the assembly's norms of silence, the teachers' presence and the large audience override his talkative disposition, which illustrates situationism, (3) The trait reading — a pure trait perspective would predict talkativeness across situations, which the assembly contradicts, (4) The correct analysis — traits and situations interact, with the situation triggering a different behavioural response from the same person. A wrong answer attributes the change solely to his trait shifting, or ignores the situational influence, revealing inability to apply the interactionist perspective.

(1) Linguistic — high, because award-winning poetry shows fluent and flexible language use, (2) Logical-mathematical and spatial — low, seen in the struggle with algebraic word problems and the inability to read maps or assemble furniture, (3) Musical — assumed average for lack of evidence, while bodily-kinaesthetic is high from learning dance choreography after a single demonstration, (4) Interpersonal — high from intuitively reading her friends' unspoken emotions, while intrapersonal and naturalistic stay average on present evidence, (5) The principle — the intelligences are relatively independent, so strength in one says nothing certain about the rest. A wrong answer forces every intelligence into high or low from overall smartness, violating the theory's core claim.

6.a: (1) The endpoint — natural killer cell cytotoxicity from blood drawn before and after exams, a biological parameter rather than self-report, (2) Reappraisal — daily guided journaling reframing threat thoughts of failing into challenge thoughts of preparation, (3) Support and sleep — a daily peer check-in with weekly teacher mentorship, plus fixed lights-out, no screens and a full night's sleep, (4) The control — a waitlist group receiving only a general exam-tips handout, (5) The pattern — the intervention group declines little while the control group declines sharply, matching the exam-season finding. A poor design takes no baseline or measures only subjective stress, missing the biological endpoint.

(1) Target behaviour — unlocking the phone to view notifications during a lecture, counted per class period, (2) Antecedents — the phone visible on the desk, alert sounds, boredom during dense slides and the fear of missing out, (3) Maintaining consequences — immediate relief from that fear, the pleasant hit of social validation, and avoidance of difficult lecture material, all of which reinforce the habit, (4) Antecedent operation — the phone goes on silent inside the bag under the seat, with a scheduled two-minute notification check before the lecture to pre-empt the urge, (5) Consequent operation — a self-monitoring log where a lecture with at most one check earns a point toward a preferred reward, while more than three checks costs points. A poor answer lists vague antecedents, omits maintaining consequences, or proposes only punishment without reinforcing the alternative behaviour.

3.a: (1) The negative automatic thought — the whole cluster of the coach hating him, never making any team and being useless at sports, which is persistent, involuntary and accepted as true, (2) The distortions — overgeneralisation from a single event, labelling himself useless, and fortune-telling about never making any team, with any one correctly named and explained earning credit, (3) The core schema — a deep enduring belief of being incompetent or inadequate, formed through earlier experiences and lying dormant until the non-selection activated it, (4) The hierarchy — schema first, then the critical incident, then situation-specific thoughts, with distortions as the thinking errors inside those thoughts. A wrong answer that calls the coach-hates-me thought a core schema confuses a deep global belief with a situation-specific one.

6.a: (1) Predisposing — family anxiety history and high neuroticism, a perfectionistic core belief, and high parental expectations in a competitive school, (2) Precipitating and perpetuating — a failed practical triggered it, while hyperventilation, catastrophically read body sensations, lab avoidance and reassuring parents maintain it, (3) The vicious cycle — the lab triggers fainting thoughts, terror and a racing heart follow, escape follows the sensations, and escape reinforces the thought she cannot cope, (4) Intervention one — interoceptive exposure with restructuring, inducing the sensations while testing the belief that dizziness means collapse, (5) Intervention two — graded behavioural experiments from visiting the empty lab to doing a simple task, dropping safety behaviours. A poor answer offers generic relaxation and positive thinking without the case-specific cycle.

3.a: (1) Plurality — five distinct groups coexist in the village, the priestly landowning caste, the herding caste, the leather-working caste, the Muslim weavers and the Christian converts, (2) Diversity — each group maintains its own rituals, deities, food habits, dress and dialect variations, (3) Caste stratification — the hierarchy runs from the Brahmin landowners through the middle-peasant Yadavs to the landless Chamars, (4) Cross-cutting line one — land ownership follows the same ladder, so economic class reinforces caste, (5) Cross-cutting line two — leather work keeps both the Chamars and their Christian converts at the bottom despite different religions, while the Muslim weavers rank above the Chamars but below the Yadavs. A student who lists only the caste ladder, or says Muslims and Christians sit outside caste, ignores how religion and class intersect and misses that conversion rarely erases caste status.

(1) First generation — landlessness forces the grandparents into bonded labour, keeping them out of school and unaware of their rights, (2) Second generation — the parents inherit landlessness and illiteracy, find only casual migratory work, pull children out of school and depend on the contractor, (3) Third generation — malnutrition stunts the daughter's cognition, attendance and performance fall, and with no mentors the dropout risk peaks, (4) Conversion point one — owning no land becomes a cultural deficit because survival labour replaces schooling, (5) Conversion point two — illiteracy becomes a social deficit when the family cannot navigate offices and banks to reach schemes. A weak answer lists hardships without the causal chain between the forms of capital.

6.a: (1) Economic — households with no land and no regularly salaried member across two generations, from land records and job-card history, (2) Cultural — adults with under five years of schooling whose own children are out of school, from census and enrolment registers, (3) Social — households with no member in any self-help group, cooperative, panchayat committee or beneficiary list, from panchayat records, (4) Political — eligible voters who never vote, never complain and never attend the gram sabha, from turnout and meeting records. Each indicator captures transmission across generations rather than a single year's status. A poor index uses only current income or attendance, missing the cumulative intergenerational logic.

3.a: (1) The right — the Forest Rights Act recognises community forest resource rights over customary common forest land within traditional village boundaries, explicitly including reserved forests, (2) The protection — no rights holder can be evicted until the recognition and verification process is complete, so the department cannot simply plant on the claimed patch, (3) The precedent — the Supreme Court's Niyamgiri judgment holds that gram sabhas in Schedule V areas decide whether a project affects their religious and cultural rights, and their consent is mandatory for forest diversion, (4) The procedure — the gram sabha has standing to file the community claim, and the mining company must obtain its consent through a resolution before diversion, failing which the project cannot proceed. A wrong answer claiming reserved forests are exempt, or that only individual claims matter, ignores the Act's inclusion of all forest categories.

4.a: (1) The displaced — Adivasis formed a large majority among those displaced by Sardar Sarovar and an even larger share by Polavaram, where hill tribes predominated, (2) Rehabilitation then — Sardar Sarovar ran under scattered state policies with no national law, so land-for-land failed and sites lacked amenities, (3) Rehabilitation now — Polavaram answers to the 2013 law mandating fair compensation, consent and impact assessment, yet stays delayed and contested, (4) Judicial role — courts allowed the Narmada rise with rehabilitation conditions under activist pressure, while newer rulings police clearances and consent, (5) The evolution — from no framework to a progressive law on paper that inertia still subverts. Saying nothing changed between the dams misses this policy evolution.

(1) AITUC — linked to the communist party, it swung between supporting provincial ministries in the late thirties and striking against the colonial state, later pursuing united-front pressure and conditional cooperation on labour legislation, (2) INTUC — founded by the Congress to anchor labour in the nationalist project, it works through tripartite institutions such as the Indian Labour Conference and avoids militant strikes that would embarrass Congress governments, as in the seventies layoff-protection amendment, (3) CITU — the Marxist party's class-struggle federation born in 1970, it rejects collaboration with the bourgeois state, mobilising general strikes and organising unorganised workers such as anganwadi and beedi workers, (4) The strategic map — legislative gains through state access for one, mass disruption for another, and united-front pressure for the third. A student who lumps all three together as left-wing unions misses this strategic divergence.

6.a: (1) The form — a worker-producer cooperative rather than a union, since no single employer exists, and it bargains over piece rates while cutting out the contractor's margin, (2) The legal lever — petition the labour commissioner for statutory minimum piece rates under the scheduled-employment notification for bidi rolling, (3) The meeting space — piggyback meetings on self-help group gatherings the women already attend, since domestic time is scarce, (4) The tangible benefit — register members for life and disability cover under the unorganised workers' law so membership pays immediately, (5) The scale — federate across village clusters, because home-based work has no workplace and a federation creates bargaining mass. A poor answer proposes registering a union, which is legally impossible without an employer.

(1) Tebhaga — Bengal, mid-forties, sharecroppers demanding two-thirds of the produce, led by the Kisan Sabha through mass non-violent mobilisation, (2) Telangana — Hyderabad, late forties, peasants and landless labourers against feudal exactions, led by the communists through armed struggle and parallel administration, (3) New farmers' movements — Punjab and Tamil Nadu from the seventies, market-involved farmers demanding prices, subsidies and waivers, organised as non-party regional blocs using blockades, (4) The inferred 2020s movement — surplus wheat, rice and sugarcane farmers demanding a legal minimum-price guarantee, non-party but electorally influential, using long sit-ins, social media and vote pressure. A poor answer copies the new-farmers row without the legal-MSP demand and newer repertoires.

(1) The Maruti Manesar struggle — contractualisation replacing permanent jobs, the same structural force as the Bombay strike's substitute-labour system, met by workers building committees outside recognised unions, (2) Gig workers' protests — platform capitalism managing informal labour through algorithms, answered by app-based collectives that mobilise digitally, (3) Scheme workers' movements — the state outsourcing welfare functions to nominally volunteer helpers on honorariums, challenged by federations demanding recognition as workers with a minimum wage, (4) The connecting thread — informalisation, contractualisation and state withdrawal link the 1982 defeat to today's struggles, and each new struggle invents organisation beyond the traditional union. A poor answer lists random strikes without identifying the structural continuity or the organisational innovation.
